Appendix B • Proofs & Comments

B.21 Geometric Formulations of Newtonian Gravity (§9.1)

The formulation of Chapter 9, Newton–Cartan theory, is one of several geometric formulations of Newtonian gravity. All of them, except the last one, live on a 4-dimensional smooth manifold with an absolute time \(t\) and a torsion-free connection with \(\nabla dt = 0\), and they differ in the additional structures and in where gravity is encoded.

Formulation Structure Connection Gravity encoded in
Newton’s absolute space \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, \nabla, t, h, \mathcal{W})\) flat, \(\nabla \mathcal{W} = 0\) force
Galilean spacetime \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, \nabla, t, h)\) flat force
Maxwellian spacetime \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, [\nabla], t, h)\) class of flat \(\nabla\) force
Newton–Cartan (Ch. 9) \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, \nabla, t)\) \(\mathrm{Ric} = 4 \pi G_N \rho \, dt \otimes dt\) connection
Bargmann structure \((\hat{\mathcal{M}}, \hat{\mathcal{O}}, \hat{\mathcal{A}}, \hat{g}, \hat{\xi})\), \(\dim \hat{\mathcal{M}} = 5\) Levi-Civita of \(\hat{g}\) metric

B.21.1 Spatial Metric

  • A spatial metric on a Newtonian spacetime \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, \nabla, t)\) assigns to every \(p \in \mathcal{M}\) an inner product on the spatial vectors at \(p\), \begin{align*} h_p : T_p\mathcal{S}_{t(p)} \times T_p\mathcal{S}_{t(p)} \xlongrightarrow{\substack{\sim \\ \sim}} \mathbb{R}, \qquad \text{symmetric and positive-definite}, \end{align*} smoothly, i.e. with smooth components \(h_{\alpha\beta} \coloneqq h(\partial x_\alpha, \partial x_\beta)\) in every stratified chart (where the \(\partial x_\alpha\) are spatial, \(dt\left\lceil \partial x_\alpha \right\rfloor = \delta^0_\alpha = 0\)). Restricted to an absolute space, \(h\) is a Riemannian metric on \(\mathcal{S}_\tau\) (Chapter 7); it is not a metric on \(\mathcal{M}\), since it only acts on spatial vectors. A stratified chart is Cartesian if \(h_{\alpha\beta} = \delta_{\alpha\beta}\).

  • \(h\) is compatible with \(\nabla\) if, for every curve \(\gamma\) and spatial vector fields \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma\) along it, \begin{align*} \frac{d}{d\lambda} \Big[ h\big( \mathcal{X}_\gamma, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma \big) \Big] = h\big( \nabla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma, \mathcal{Y}_\gamma \big) + h\big( \mathcal{X}_\gamma, \nabla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{Y}_\gamma \big), \end{align*} where \(\nabla_{v_\gamma} \mathcal{X}_\gamma\) is spatial because \(\nabla dt = 0\). In a Cartesian stratified chart this leaves exactly5 \begin{align*} \Gamma^\alpha_{0\beta} = \Gamma^\alpha_{\beta0} = - \Gamma^\beta_{0\alpha}, \qquad \Gamma^\alpha_{00} \text{ arbitrary}, \qquad \text{all other } \Gamma^i_{jk} = 0. \end{align*}

  • No Levi-Civita connection. Unlike a metric on \(\mathcal{M}\), the pair \((t, h)\) does not determine \(\nabla\): six component functions remain free, the antisymmetric \(\Gamma^\alpha_{0\beta}\) (rotation of the axes w.r.t. parallel transport) and \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00}\) (acceleration of free fall). These are precisely the slots of the pseudo-forces and of gravity in Section 9.4, so in every formulation below \(\nabla\) is an independent datum.

B.21.2 Formulations

  • Galilean spacetime is a sextuple \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, \nabla, t, h)\) such that

    1. \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, \nabla, t)\) is a Newtonian spacetime (Section 9.1), in particular \(\dim \mathcal{M} = 4\);

    2. \(h\) is a spatial metric compatible with \(\nabla\);

    3. \(\nabla\) is flat, \(\mathrm{Riem} = 0\).

    Each absolute space is then a Euclidean 3-space, but nothing identifies spatial points at different times: space is not a single 3-manifold. Around every point there are Cartesian stratified charts with \(\Gamma = 0\), the inertial charts6. If two charts are inertial, the transformation law (Chapter 6) reduces to \(\frac{\partial \mathscr{Y}^i}{\partial \mathscr{X}^s} \frac{\partial^2 \mathscr{X}^s}{\partial \mathscr{Y}^k \partial \mathscr{Y}^j} = 0\), so the transition map is affine, and preserving \(h_{\alpha\beta} = \delta_{\alpha\beta}\) makes it a Galilean transformation \begin{align*} \xi^\alpha = R^\alpha{}_\beta \, \eta^\beta + v^\alpha \, t + a^\alpha, \qquad R \text{ a constant rotation matrix}, \; v^\alpha, a^\alpha \text{ constants}. \end{align*} (Without \(h\), \(R\) would be any constant invertible matrix.) Gravity is a force: worldlines of particles falling under gravity satisfy \begin{align*} \nabla_{v_\gamma} v_\gamma = - \mathrm{grad}\,\phi, \qquad \Delta \phi = 4 \pi G_N \rho, \end{align*} where the gradient is the spatial vector field with \(h\big( \mathrm{grad}\,\phi, \mathcal{Y} \big) = d\phi\left\lceil \mathcal{Y} \right\rfloor\) for every spatial \(\mathcal{Y}\), with component functions \(\partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil\) in a Cartesian chart, and \(\Delta \phi \coloneqq \sum_\alpha \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil \right\rceil\) there. Free fall is not autoparallel, and the cancellation of \(m\) is a property of the force law, not of the geometry.

  • Newton’s absolute space is a septuple \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, \nabla, t, h, \mathcal{W})\) formed by a Galilean spacetime and a vector field \(\mathcal{W} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}\) with7 \begin{align*} dt\left\lceil \mathcal{W} \right\rfloor = 1, \qquad \nabla \mathcal{W} = 0. \end{align*} The integral curves of \(\mathcal{W}\) are the points of space at rest. They identify all absolute spaces with a single Euclidean 3-space \(E^3\), so that \(\mathcal{M} \cong \mathbb{R} \times E^3\), and they single out the inertial charts adapted to \(\mathcal{W} = \partial x_0\), those with \(v = 0\). No experiment detects this distinction (Galilean relativity), so \(\mathcal{W}\) is superfluous structure.

  • Maxwellian spacetime is a sextuple \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, [\nabla], t, h)\) in which the connection of a Galilean spacetime is replaced by an equivalence class of flat connections, each making \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, \nabla, t, h)\) a Galilean spacetime, with \begin{align*} \nabla' \sim \nabla \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \nabla'_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} = \nabla_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} + dt\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor \, dt\left\lceil \mathcal{Y} \right\rfloor \, \mathcal{K}, \qquad \forall \, \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{Y} \in \Gamma T\mathcal{M}, \end{align*} for some spatial vector field \(\mathcal{K}\) with \(\nabla_\mathcal{Y} \mathcal{K} = 0\) for every spatial \(\mathcal{Y}\), i.e. whose component functions in a Cartesian inertial chart depend on \(t\) only. Equivalent connections differ only in \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00}\), by \(\mathcal{K}^\alpha(t)\): the class retains a standard of rotation (\(\Gamma^\alpha_{0\beta} = 0\)) but no standard of linear acceleration. The distinguished charts are related by \(\xi^\alpha = R^\alpha{}_\beta \, \eta^\beta + b^\alpha(t)\), with \(R\) constant and \(b^\alpha\) arbitrary, and the potential is only defined up to \(\phi \to \phi + \sum_\alpha \ddot{b}^\alpha(t) \, \xi^\alpha\): a spatially uniform gravitational field is indistinguishable from an accelerated choice of charts8.

  • Newton–Cartan theory and the Trautman–Künzle conditions. Adding to the Newtonian spacetime of Chapter 9 a compatible spatial metric gives a sextuple \((\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}, \mathcal{A}, \nabla, t, h)\) as for Galilean spacetime, with flatness replaced by the field equation \(\mathrm{Ric} = 4 \pi G_N \rho \, dt \otimes dt\). Every Galilean spacetime and potential \(\phi\) yield such a structure by geometrization, \begin{align*} \nabla_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} \coloneqq \nabla^0_\mathcal{X} \mathcal{Y} + dt\left\lceil \mathcal{X} \right\rfloor \, dt\left\lceil \mathcal{Y} \right\rfloor \, \mathrm{grad}\,\phi, \end{align*} with \(\nabla^0\) the flat connection, which in a Cartesian inertial chart of \(\nabla^0\) is the connection of Subsection 9.5. The converse fails: the field equation constrains only the Ricci curvature, and also admits non-Newtonian solutions, e.g. Coriolis-type fields whose rotation rate varies in space. A Newton–Cartan connection arises locally by geometrization if and only if, in Cartesian stratified charts, \begin{align*} \text{(TK1)} \quad \mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{\beta\delta0} = 0, \qquad\qquad \text{(TK2)} \quad \mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{0\beta0} = \mathrm{Riem}^\beta_{0\alpha0}, \end{align*} the Trautman–Künzle conditions9. In Chapter 9 they hold by construction: there \(\Gamma^\alpha_{0\beta} = 0\) and \(\mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{0\beta0} = \partial x_\beta\left\lfloor \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil \right\rceil\). Moreover, the pair \((\nabla^0, \phi)\) is fixed by \(\nabla\) only up to the Maxwellian equivalence above: Newton–Cartan theory determines a Maxwellian spacetime, not a Galilean one.

  • Bargmann structure is a quintuple \((\hat{\mathcal{M}}, \hat{\mathcal{O}}, \hat{\mathcal{A}}, \hat{g}, \hat{\xi})\), with \(\hat{\mathcal{M}}\) a 5-dimensional smooth manifold, \(\hat{g}\) a Lorentzian metric (Chapter 7) and \(\hat{\xi} \in \Gamma T\hat{\mathcal{M}}\) a nowhere-vanishing vector field which is null and parallel, \begin{align*} \hat{g}(\hat{\xi}, \hat{\xi}) = 0, \qquad \hat{\nabla} \hat{\xi} = 0, \end{align*} w.r.t. the Levi-Civita connection \(\hat{\nabla}\) of \(\hat{g}\). The 4-dimensional space of integral curves of \(\hat{\xi}\) inherits a Newton–Cartan structure, with \(dt\) induced by \(\flat(\hat{\xi})\) (Duval, Burdet, Künzle and Perrin, 1985). For instance, with coordinates \((\mathscr{X}^0, \dots, \mathscr{X}^4)\), \(\mathscr{X}^0 = t\), and \(\hat{\xi} = \partial x_4\), \begin{align*} \hat{g} = dt \otimes dx^4 + dx^4 \otimes dt + \textstyle\sum_\alpha dx^\alpha \otimes dx^\alpha - 2 \phi \; dt \otimes dt, \qquad \flat(\partial x_4) = dt, \end{align*} whose geodesics project onto the free-fall worldlines (Eisenhart, 1929). Gravity is encoded in a metric and its Levi-Civita connection, as in General Relativity, at the price of a fifth dimension.

B.21.3 Remarks

  • Inertial systems. Defining an inertial system as one in which free particles move uniformly along straight lines, and stating Newton I “in an inertial system”, is nearly circular. In Section 9.2, Newton I is chart independent: a single connection has all free worldlines as autoparallels. Inertial charts, \(\Gamma = 0\), become a derived notion: they are adapted to an inertial frame \(\mathcal{W} = \partial x_0\), \(\nabla \mathcal{W} = 0\), and exist on an open set if and only if \(\mathrm{Riem} = 0\) there. With non-uniform gravity only charts with \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00} = 0\) along a single freely falling worldline remain (Subsection 9.5.2).

  • Is Newtonian spacetime curved? It depends on which connection describes free motion: \(\nabla^0\) (Galilean, flat) or \(\nabla\) (Newton–Cartan, curved wherever there are tidal accelerations). Both predict the same motion, but Newton–Cartan theory is preferable: \(\nabla\) is fixed by free fall whereas \(\nabla^0\) is not; the universality of free fall is built in, since \(m\) never enters \(\nabla\); and the field equation is local, whereas Poisson’s equation needs boundary conditions which cannot be imposed for a homogeneous mass distribution filling space (Neumann–Seeliger paradox). The curvature is of a restricted kind: the absolute spaces are flat, \(\mathrm{Riem}^\alpha_{\beta\delta\kappa} = 0\).

B.21.4 Laplace’s Question: Space versus Spacetime

  • Is there a connection on space whose autoparallels, \(\ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U} + \Gamma^\alpha_{\beta\delta} \, \dot{\gamma}^\beta_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^\delta_\mathcal{U} = 0\), are the free-fall trajectories \(\ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U} = - \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil\)? No:

    1. Velocity dependence: the \(\Gamma\)-term is quadratic in the velocity, \(\partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil\) does not depend on it. An autoparallel with vanishing velocity has vanishing acceleration, but a stone released at rest falls.

    2. Reparametrization: with \(\gamma\), also \(\lambda \mapsto \gamma(c \, \lambda)\), \(c \neq 0\), is an autoparallel, so the path depends only on the initial point and direction. Stones thrown in the same direction with different speeds, however, follow different parabolas.

  • On spacetime the answer is yes, because the speed becomes part of the direction: with \(\dot{\gamma}^0_\mathcal{U} = 1\), the free-fall equation reads \(\ddot{\gamma}^\alpha_\mathcal{U} + \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil \dot{\gamma}^0_\mathcal{U} \, \dot{\gamma}^0_\mathcal{U} = 0\), the autoparallel equation with \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00} = \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil\). A stone at rest has spacetime velocity \((1, 0, 0, 0)\), on which \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00}\) acts, and different speeds are different spacetime directions. The same mechanism absorbs any acceleration of degree \(0\), \(1\) or \(2\) in the spatial velocity, through \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00}\), \(\Gamma^\alpha_{0\beta}\) and \(\Gamma^\alpha_{\beta\delta}\), provided it is the same for all particles. The Lorentz force is not, since it depends on \(q/m\); Kaluza–Klein theory absorbs it by turning \(q/m\) into a velocity component in a fifth dimension.

5

\(\Gamma^0_{jk} = 0\) by \(\nabla dt = 0\). Inserting \(\mathcal{X}_\gamma = \partial x_\alpha \circ \gamma\), \(\mathcal{Y}_\gamma = \partial x_\beta \circ \gamma\) for arbitrary \(\gamma\) gives \(\Gamma^\beta_{\alpha k} = - \Gamma^\alpha_{\beta k}\). For \(k = 0\), with torsion-freeness, this is the antisymmetry of \(\Gamma^\alpha_{0\beta} = \Gamma^\alpha_{\beta0}\). For \(k = \delta\) spatial, alternating it with the symmetry in the lower indices, \(\Gamma^\alpha_{\beta\delta} = - \Gamma^\beta_{\alpha\delta} = - \Gamma^\beta_{\delta\alpha} = \Gamma^\delta_{\beta\alpha} = \Gamma^\delta_{\alpha\beta} = - \Gamma^\alpha_{\delta\beta} = - \Gamma^\alpha_{\beta\delta}\), so \(\Gamma^\alpha_{\beta\delta} = 0\). \(\square\)

6

A classical result, whose proof we omit: flatness gives charts with \(\Gamma = 0\), in which compatibility makes the \(h_{\alpha\beta}\) constant, and a constant linear change of the spatial coordinates makes them \(\delta_{\alpha\beta}\).

7

Often called Newtonian spacetime in the literature, not to be confused with Section 9.1.

8

This is Corollary VI of the Principia. See J. Earman, World Enough and Space-Time, MIT Press (1989); S. Saunders, Rethinking Newton’s Principia, Philosophy of Science 80 (2013) 22–48.

9

Sketch. By (TK1), \(\Gamma^\alpha_{0\beta}\) depends on \(t\) only, and a time-dependent rotation of the axes removes it (Subsection 9.4). In the new chart, (TK2) reads \(\partial x_\beta\left\lfloor \Gamma^\alpha_{00} \right\rceil = \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \Gamma^\beta_{00} \right\rceil\), so on any ball \(\Gamma^\alpha_{00} = \partial x_\alpha\left\lfloor \phi \right\rceil\) for some \(\phi\), and \(\nabla^0\) is the connection whose coefficients vanish in this chart. See D. Malament, Topics in the Foundations of General Relativity and Newtonian Gravitation Theory, University of Chicago Press (2012), Chapter 4.
